guided_reading.book_title: From Rotting Hulks to Sandstone Rock: The First Fleet Reaches Warrane (1787–1788)
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub · Historical Story (1783–1788)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original true historical story tracing convict transportation from Portsmouth’s prison hulks to Gadigal Country at Warrane (Sydney Cove) in January 1788.
guided_reading.author_context: When America won independence in 1783, Britain lost its old dumping ground for convicts. Overcrowded floating prisons in Portsmouth and the Thames pushed Westminster to gamble on a penal colony 15,000 miles away in New South Wales.
guided_reading.cover_caption: Francis Wheatley’s 1786 oil portrait of Captain Arthur Phillip RN holding a rolled 1787 plan of New South Wales before sailing with the First Fleet.

vocabVault.def: Britain’s harsh 18th-century criminal laws punishing over 200 offences with death or overseas transportation.
Rotting, mastless wooden warships anchored in Portsmouth Harbour and the Thames as overcrowded floating jails.
The Gadigal clan’s ancestral cove in Port Jackson, renamed Sydney Cove by Arthur Phillip in January 1788.
The First Nations clan of the Eora Nation whose Country surrounds Warrane (Sydney Harbour).

guided_reading.extract:
Before dawn on 13 May 1787, heavy leg-irons clanked below the waterline in Portsmouth Harbour. Since losing its thirteen American colonies in 1783, Britain had nowhere to ship prisoners sentenced under its harsh "Bloody Code." Thousands of men, women, and children—some jailed for stealing bread or a handkerchief—shivered aboard damp, disease-ridden warships known as prison hulks.

That May morning, Captain Arthur Phillip led eleven small wooden vessels out into the Channel. Packed below decks sailed more than 730 convicts bound for the far side of the earth. For eight gruelling months, the First Fleet pitched across fifteen thousand miles of ocean.

When the ships reached Botany Bay in January 1788, Phillip saw straight away that Joseph Banks had been wrong. The bay was shallow, exposed to gales, and short of fresh water. Exploring just north into Port Jackson, Phillip found what he called "the finest harbour in the world"—a deep sheltered cove known to its Gadigal custodians as Warrane.

On 26 January 1788, marines raised the Union Jack at Sydney Cove. Survival, however, hung by a thread. Cheap axes from English contractors bent against giant red gum trees and hard sandstone, leaving jailers and convicts alike facing starvation on Gadigal Country.

parent_discussion.question: How did losing the thirteen American colonies in 1783 lead to the First Fleet sailing from Portsmouth in May 1787?
parent_discussion.answer: Britain had nowhere left to ship prisoners sentenced under the "Bloody Code," so thousands shivered aboard damp, disease-ridden prison hulks until Captain Arthur Phillip sailed eleven ships and over 730 convicts to the far side of the earth.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Captain Arthur Phillip abandon Botany Bay after arriving in January 1788?
parent_discussion.answer: Botany Bay was shallow, exposed to gales, and short of fresh water, so Phillip sailed north into Port Jackson to a deep, sheltered cove called Warrane by its Gadigal custodians.

parent_discussion.question: Raising the Union Jack at Sydney Cove sounded like a triumph, yet survival "hung by a thread"—why did both convicts and their jailers face such a desperate struggle?
parent_discussion.answer: After an eight-month voyage across fifteen thousand miles of ocean, cheap axes from English contractors bent against giant red gum trees and hard sandstone, leaving everyone facing starvation on Gadigal Country.

story_check.question: What were the "prison hulks" moored in Portsmouth Harbour and the River Thames?
options: Decommissioned wooden warships used as overcrowded floating prisons
Luxury passenger clippers bound for Sydney
story_check.feedback: After losing its thirteen American colonies in 1783, Britain crammed thousands of convicts into rotting, mastless old warships called prison hulks.

story_check.question: Why did Arthur Phillip move the First Fleet north from Botany Bay to Port Jackson (Warrane)?
options: He discovered rich gold mines at Ballarat
Botany Bay was shallow, windswept, and lacked enough fresh water
He had orders to return to Portsmouth
story_check.feedback: Botany Bay lacked safe deep shelter and fresh water, whereas Warrane in Port Jackson offered both.

story_check.question: What happened when people at Sydney Cove tried to clear land using axes supplied by English contractors?
options: They cleared lush farmland in two weeks
Cheap metal tools bent and broke against giant red gum trees and sandstone
Gadigal elders traded steel ploughs with them
story_check.feedback: Cheap axes from English contractors bent against giant red gum trees and hard sandstone, leaving jailers and convicts facing starvation.

monday_cold_call.answer: Losing America closed Britain’s old convict ports, overflowing prison hulks in Portsmouth and the Thames until the First Fleet landed convicts on Gadigal land at Sydney Cove.

guided_reading.book_title: The Warrior Who Defied Muskets: Pemulwuy’s Twelve-Year Eora War (1790–1802)
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub · Historical Story (1789–1802)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original true historical story grounded in First Fleet chronicles (David Collins, 1798) and Governor King’s dispatches on smallpox, Bennelong, and Pemulwuy.
guided_reading.author_context: After devastating smallpox struck Sydney Harbour in April 1789, Eora leaders fought for survival in contrasting ways. While Wangal diplomat Bennelong sought negotiation, Bidjigal warrior Pemulwuy waged a twelve-year guerrilla campaign defending Eora Country.
guided_reading.cover_caption: 1798 London engraving depicting a Bidjigal/Eora warrior poised in a tied bark canoe raising a fishing spear along the waters of the Sydney basin.

vocabVault.def: Bidjigal resistance leader who led a twelve-year guerrilla war (1790–1802) defending Eora land around Sydney.
Wangal elder and diplomat who learned English and sailed to London (1792) hoping to broker respect between cultures.
The Eora word for the catastrophic April 1789 smallpox outbreak that killed roughly half of Sydney’s Indigenous clans.
Pemulwuy’s Eora/Dharug clan whose hunting grounds stretched from Botany Bay toward Parramatta.

guided_reading.extract:
Fifteen months after the First Fleet anchored at Sydney Cove, silent terror swept the harbour. In April 1789, a deadly wave of smallpox—called galgalla by the Eora—killed at least half the First Nations people around Port Jackson. Empty bark canoes drifted into quiet bays as elders and song-keepers died with no natural defence against the new sickness.

Amid that grief, two Eora men chose opposite paths to save their clans. Wangal elder Woollarawarre Bennelong learned English, dined with Governor Phillip, and sailed to London in 1792 hoping talks would win respect. Bidjigal warrior Pemulwuy saw British fences swallowing yam beds and kangaroo plains, so he chose war.

From 1790 onward, Pemulwuy led a bold twelve-year bush campaign along the Parramatta and Hawkesbury rivers. Knowing spears could not beat massed muskets in open lines, his men set fire to ripe cornfields and drove off settlers’ sheep.

In March 1797, during fierce fighting at Parramatta, seven buckshot pellets tore into Pemulwuy’s head and chest. Chained to a hospital bed under guard, the wounded leader waited for night. He slipped out into the bush wearing a heavy leg-iron on his ankle and fought on. Across Sydney, awed fighters believed no British bullet could kill Pemulwuy—until an ambush ended his life in 1802.

parent_discussion.question: How did the April 1789 smallpox outbreak (galgalla) devastate Eora society right before frontier farms expanded?
parent_discussion.answer: Because Eora clans had no natural defence against smallpox, at least half the people around Port Jackson died—including elders and song-keepers.

parent_discussion.question: Compare Woollarawarre Bennelong and Pemulwuy: how did these two Eora leaders choose opposite paths to defend their clans?
parent_discussion.answer: Bennelong learned English, dined with Governor Phillip, and sailed to London hoping talks would win respect, while Pemulwuy fought a twelve-year bush war to stop British fences swallowing yam beds and kangaroo plains.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Pemulwuy target ripe cornfields and settlers’ sheep instead of fighting British muskets in the open—and why did his 1797 escape make him a legend?
parent_discussion.answer: He knew spears could not beat massed muskets in open lines, so burning crops and driving off sheep struck at the expanding farms; surviving seven buckshot pellets and escaping hospital wearing a leg-iron convinced people no British bullet could kill him.

story_check.question: Roughly what share of the Eora people around Sydney Harbour died in the April 1789 smallpox outbreak?
options: At least half of the local Eora population
story_check.feedback: Having zero prior exposure to smallpox, at least 50% of the Sydney basin’s Eora population perished in 1789.

story_check.question: What targets did Pemulwuy’s fighters strike along the Parramatta and Hawkesbury rivers?
options: Ripening colonial cornfields and settlers’ livestock
story_check.feedback: Pemulwuy targeted colonial crops and sheep to halt farm expansion onto Bidjigal yam and hunting grounds.

story_check.question: What happened after Pemulwuy was hit by seven buckshot pellets at Parramatta in March 1797?
options: He sailed to London with Governor Phillip
He surrendered and signed a treaty
He escaped from hospital into the bush with a leg-iron still on his ankle
story_check.feedback: Pemulwuy survived seven buckshot wounds and slipped out of hospital into the bush wearing a heavy leg-iron, becoming a legend across Sydney.

monday_cold_call.question: Why did Pemulwuy become a legend across Sydney after the fierce fighting at Parramatta in March 1797?
monday_cold_call.answer: He survived seven buckshot pellets to his head and chest and escaped hospital chains wearing a leg-iron, convincing followers British bullets could not kill him.

guided_reading.book_title: "Clancy of the Overflow" (1889) & "Waltzing Matilda" (1895): Bush Myths vs Frontier Reality
guided_reading.author: A. B. "Banjo" Paterson (1889–1895)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Verbatim public-domain stanzas from Banjo Paterson’s 1889 and 1895 Australian bush ballads framed against pastoral dispossession and Tasmania’s Black War.
guided_reading.author_context: Poet Andrew Barton "Banjo" Paterson wrote Australia’s best-known bush ballads celebrating outback drovers, swagmen, and sheep stations. Historians read his verse alongside frontier archives to see both settler bush pride and the silenced dispossession of First Nations Country.
guided_reading.cover_caption: Charles Woolley’s 1866 Hobart studio portrait of Nuennonne diplomat and Black War survivor Truganini; note the colonial album mount’s false "Last of..." label.

vocabVault.def: Nineteenth-century Australian bush poet who wrote "Clancy of the Overflow" (1889) and "Waltzing Matilda" (1895).
A wealthy colonial grazier who seized huge inland tracts of Aboriginal Country to run Merino sheep.
An Australian river waterhole—adopted from Wiradjuri language—vital to both Aboriginal clans and pastoral flocks.
Nuennonne woman of Tasmania who endured the Black War (1824–1831) and forced exile at Wybalenna on Flinders Island.

guided_reading.extract:
Across the nineteenth century, wealthy colonial "squatters" drove millions of Merino sheep inland to supply British wool mills. Bush ballads by poet Banjo Paterson painted those vast sheep runs as a romantic world of sunlit plains and free-spirited drovers:
Banjo Paterson, "Clancy of the Overflow" (1889):
In my wild erratic fancy visions come to me of Clancy
Gone a-droving "down the Cooper" where the western drovers go;
As the stock are slowly stringing, Clancy rides behind them singing,
For the drover’s life has pleasures that the townsfolk never know.
And the bush hath friends to meet him, and their kindly voices greet him
In the murmur of the breezes and the river on its bars,
And he sees the vision splendid of the sunlit plains extended,
And at night the wondrous glory of the everlasting stars.
Banjo Paterson, "Waltzing Matilda" (1895):
Down came a jumbuck to drink at that billabong,
Up jumped the swagman and grabbed him with glee...
Up rode the squatter, mounted on his thoroughbred,
Down came the troopers, one, two, three.
Yet notice who vanishes from those famous bush verses. Every "sunlit plain" and billabong was stolen Aboriginal Country. Squatters’ sheep triggered Tasmania’s brutal Black War—survived by Nuennonne diplomat Truganini—and mainland massacres like Myall Creek in 1838.

parent_discussion.question: How does Banjo Paterson make the drover’s life sound so free and joyful in "Clancy of the Overflow"?
parent_discussion.answer: He pictures Clancy riding and singing behind his livestock with pleasures "townsfolk never know," surrounded by friendly breezes, sunlit plains, and everlasting stars.

parent_discussion.question: Who holds power in the bush according to "Waltzing Matilda", and what drove squatters so deep inland?
parent_discussion.answer: The wealthy squatter mounted on his thoroughbred backed by three troopers holds the power, and squatters pushed inland with millions of Merino sheep to supply British wool mills.

parent_discussion.question: Look at the contrast between Banjo Paterson’s sunlit verses and the final paragraph—who vanishes from these famous bush poems, and why does that matter?
parent_discussion.answer: First Nations peoples disappear from the poems even though every "sunlit plain" and billabong was stolen Aboriginal Country—hiding Tasmania’s brutal Black War, Truganini’s exile, and mainland massacres like Myall Creek in 1838.

story_check.question: In Banjo Paterson’s 1889 ballad, what job is Clancy doing "down the Cooper"?
story_check.feedback: Clancy is a drover herding livestock across vast western plains.

story_check.question: In "Waltzing Matilda", who rides up alongside three police troopers to confront the swagman by the billabong?
options: The wealthy squatter mounted on his thoroughbred
story_check.feedback: The squatter—who controlled vast pastoral runs and waterholes—arrives on his thoroughbred with armed troopers.

story_check.question: What harsh reality of pastoral expansion is left out of Paterson’s romantic bush ballads?
options: Violent dispossession of First Nations peoples in Tasmania’s Black War and Myall Creek
The price of wool in Britain
story_check.feedback: Romantic settler ballads left out the violent seizure of Aboriginal Country, waterholes, and lives.

monday_cold_call.question: What does Banjo Paterson celebrate about the Australian bush, and what crucial frontier truth do his ballads leave out?
monday_cold_call.answer: He celebrates sunlit plains, drovers, and billabongs, while silencing how squatters’ Merino sheep runs violently dispossessed First Nations clans in Tasmania and on the mainland.

Think: Which word in "Waltzing Matilda" actually comes from an Aboriginal language?

guided_reading.book_title: The Eureka Stockade: The Bakery Hill Oath & Fight for Democracy (1854–1855)
guided_reading.author: Raffaello Carboni (Melbourne, 1855 · State Library Victoria)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Adapted from Italian gold-digger Raffaello Carboni’s 1855 eyewitness memoir The Eureka Stockade, calibrated for crisp Year 8 aloud reading.
guided_reading.author_context: Gold discoveries in 1851 tripled Australia’s settler population within a decade. Outraged by expensive monthly Gold Licences enforced at sword-point while miners lacked the vote, Italian digger Raffaello Carboni stood beside Irishman Peter Lalor beneath the Southern Cross flag at Ballarat in 1854.
guided_reading.cover_caption: Edwin Stocqueler’s oil painting Australian Gold Diggings (c. 1855, National Library of Australia), showing prospectors panning in creek mud beside canvas tents and goldfield stores.

vocabVault.def: Italian-born Ballarat miner and translator whose 1855 eyewitness book preserved the Eureka Stockade oath.
The rough timber barricade built by Ballarat gold miners in Victoria and stormed by British troops on 3 December 1854.
The hated thirty-shilling monthly tax every miner had to pay whether they found gold or dug empty clay.
Private voting on printed official papers—pioneered in Australia in 1856 right after Eureka and later copied worldwide.

guided_reading.extract:
Italian-born prospector Raffaello Carboni dug for gold at Ballarat in Victoria. In 1855, he published his eyewitness book about armed police "licence hunts" and the rebel oath sworn beneath the Southern Cross flag.

"Whether a digger struck rich gold in wet clay or worked an empty hole for weeks, the Commissioners showed no mercy. Twice a week, mounted troopers rode in with drawn swords shouting, ’Traps! Show your licences!’ Any miner caught without his thirty-shilling monthly paper was chained to a gum tree at the camp. It was taxation at the point of a bayonet upon men denied a single vote!

"On 29 November 1854, twelve thousand diggers of twenty nations met on Bakery Hill. As the blue-and-white Southern Cross flag unfurled overhead, we burned our hated licences on bonfires. Next afternoon, Peter Lalor knelt bareheaded beneath that flag, raised his right hand, and led five hundred diggers in a solemn oath.

"’We swear by the Southern Cross to stand truly by each other, and fight to defend our rights and liberties!’

"At dawn on Sunday 3 December, three hundred soldiers and police stormed our timber stockade, killing at least twenty-two diggers. Thirteen of us were dragged to Melbourne for High Treason trials. Yet citizen juries cheered and freed every single prisoner—winning white male votes and the secret ballot within eighteen months."

parent_discussion.question: Why did Raffaello Carboni call the Victorian Gold Licence "taxation at the point of a bayonet"?
parent_discussion.answer: Every digger had to pay thirty shillings a month whether they found gold or worked an empty hole, faced twice-weekly raids by troopers with drawn swords, and had zero right to vote.

parent_discussion.question: How did the Eureka diggers lose the dawn battle on 3 December 1854 yet still win a major political victory within eighteen months?
parent_discussion.answer: Although troops stormed the stockade and killed at least twenty-two diggers, Melbourne citizen juries cheered and freed all thirteen prisoners tried for High Treason—helping win white male votes and the secret ballot.

parent_discussion.question: Carboni noted that twelve thousand diggers of "twenty nations" stood together on Bakery Hill, yet the reforms won "white male votes"—what does that show about both the strength and the limits of Eureka’s victory?
parent_discussion.answer: Miners from around the world united against unfair armed raids to win the secret ballot, yet voting rights were still limited to white men—leaving women and non-white people shut out.

story_check.question: How much did a Victorian Gold Licence cost each month, and who had to pay it?
options: Only miners who found large gold nuggets paid ten pounds
Thirty shillings every month, whether a miner found gold or nothing at all
One shilling a year for storekeepers only
story_check.feedback: Every digger had to buy a 30-shilling paper licence every month regardless of whether they struck gold.

story_check.question: Beneath which flag did Peter Lalor and five hundred diggers swear their oath at Ballarat?
story_check.feedback: Miners swore by the blue-and-white Southern Cross flag to stand truly by each other and defend their rights.

story_check.question: What happened when Raffaello Carboni and twelve other Eureka rebels were tried for High Treason in Melbourne?
options: They were transported to Portsmouth hulks
Citizen juries acquitted every single prisoner, forcing democratic reforms
They were fined thirty shillings each
The Gold Licence fee was doubled
story_check.feedback: Sympathetic Melbourne citizen juries cheered and freed all thirteen prisoners, helping win white male votes and Australia’s 1856 secret ballot.

monday_cold_call.question: How did the Eureka Stockade miners lose the dawn battle on 3 December 1854 yet win the political struggle?
monday_cold_call.answer: Although three hundred soldiers and police stormed the stockade and killed at least twenty-two diggers, Melbourne citizen juries freed all thirteen treason prisoners, leading to white male votes and the secret ballot within eighteen months.

Pair: Contrast how European miners won voting rights after 1854 with how Chinese miners and Aboriginal Australians were treated up to 1901.

cover_caption: Francis Fowkes’s Sketch and Description of the Settlement at Sydney Cove, Port Jackson (16 April 1788), the earliest chart of Britain’s First Fleet penal colony on ancestral Gadigal Country.

teacher_guidance_overview.curriculum_focus: KS3 National Curriculum: Ideas, political power, industry and empire — Britain, 1745–1901 (settler colonialism, First Nations custodianship, penal transportation, frontier resistance, and democratic Federation).
teacher_guidance_overview.disciplinary_threads: Causation and Consequence, Evidential Source Scrutiny, Historical Interpretations, and Significance.
teacher_guidance_overview.non_specialist_summary: This five-enquiry sequence traces how over 65,000 years of continuous First Nations custodianship collided with British imperial expansion after James Cook's 1770 coastal claim and the 1788 arrival of the First Fleet. Pupils investigate convict life, epidemic disease, diplomatic mediation and armed resistance across the Sydney Basin and Van Diemen's Land, and the Merino wool land grab. The unit concludes with the 1851 Gold Rush, the 1854 Eureka Stockade, the 1901 White Australia Policy, and First Nations civil rights campaigning culminating in the 1992 Mabo ruling.
